blurb: West Berlin's first acid/techno basement; Interfisch, Dr. Motte, Tanith.

name: vurt.
blurb: Techno club beneath a karaoke bar in Hapjeong, founded in 2014 under the slogan Ancient Future.
skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass

name: WHITE Dubai
blurb: Club at Meydan run by Addmind, holding about 2,000, with a top-20 DJ Mag placing; a seated dinner venue under Covid rules by November 2020.

name: Zhao Dai
blurb: Beijing techno club opened in 2017; shut eight months by the 2022 lockdown, reopened December 2022.

name: Arcadia
blurb: Pip Rush and Bertie Cole's company, builders of the Afterburner, the 50-tonne Spider (2010) and the Dragonfly (2024) at Glastonbury.

name: Boy Better Know
blurb: Independent label and crew founded by brothers Skepta and Jme Adenuga in north London.

name: Camp Question Mark
blurb: Burning Man bass camp at 2:00 running PK Sound rigs for peak crowds of 10,000 to 15,000, by Mixmag's account.

name: Distruction Boyz
blurb: Durban duo Que and Goldmax, producers of Babes Wodumo's 'Wololo', makers of 'Omunye' and of the 2017 album 'Gqom Is the Future'.

name: Furacão 2000
blurb: Rio sound system and producer, merged from Som 2000 and Guarani 2000, behind the Tornado Muito Nervoso compilations and Gaiola das Popozudas.

name: Honey Soundsystem
blurb: Party crew and label founded by Jacob Sperber and Ken Woodard, curators of Patrick Cowley's archive and of Tea With Honey and Deviants.

name: Jazar Crew
blurb: Haifa collective of five friends, throwing parties from 2011, who played Boiler Room's first Palestine broadcast in 2018.

name: SFX Entertainment / LiveStyle
blurb: Robert Sillerman's dance-event roll-up, bankrupt in 2016 and renamed LiveStyle; sold ID&T to Superstruct in 2021.

name: Mayan Warrior
blurb: Pablo González Vargas's Mexico City art car, at Burning Man from 2012; destroyed by fire in 2023 and rebuilt for 2024.

name: Opulent Temple
blurb: Burning Man sound camp from 2003, with a flame-throwing DJ booth; its big-name guests were not paid, Syd Gris said in 2014.

name: Pxssy Palace
blurb: London queer collective known for tiered ticketing, a trained support team and calling its spaces 'intentional' rather than 'safe'.

name: Robot Heart
blurb: Art car built on a 1972 Leland double-decker bus, on the playa since 2008; its camp numbered 90 to 100 people in 2024.

name: SIREN
blurb: Five-member London collective running parties, a zine, workshops and an online platform for marginalised people in nightlife.

name: SubDub
blurb: Leeds bass night with Iration Steppas as resident system; its crew put together the first Outlook festival in 2008.

name: The Carry Nation
blurb: Party formed by Will Automagic and Nita Aviance, named for the temperance campaigner; a monthly at Good Room in Brooklyn.

name: WAIFU
blurb: Queer and femme collective formed in 2019 after a trans woman was refused entry to a Ni-chōme party.

name: Adonis
blurb: Queer rave started by Shay Malt in Tottenham, with Hannah Holland and Grace Sands as residents and a vibe-based door.

name: Analog Room
blurb: Dubai club night founded by the Iranian promoter Mehdi Ansari, which booked only local performers for a year and brought Mutek to the city.

name: Astroworld Festival, 2021
blurb: Houston festival where a crowd surge killed ten on 5 November 2021; no indictments, wrongful-death suits settled by May 2024.

name: AVA Festival
blurb: Sarah McBriar's Audio Visual Arts festival in Belfast, begun as a one-day event in 2014; Titanic Slipways in 2026.

name: Back to the Future
blurb: Dave Roberts's 1989 party series, run alongside Sunrise: grain silos in Hampshire that April, then a joint festival with Sunrise at Longwick in August.

name: Muzik
blurb: IPC's dance monthly: the Muzik Awards, the serious long reads of the superclub years.

name: The Wire
blurb: The experimental monthly that took techno seriously as music in the 1990s; Kodwo Eshun and Simon Reynolds's writing.

name: A-1 Record Shop
blurb: Second-hand shop at 439 East 6th Street, founded by Isaac Kosman; a hip-hop producers' digging spot whose staff included Ron Morelli and Daniel Wang.
q: "A-1 Record Shop" New York record shop

name: Boogie Times
blurb: Romford: Danny Donnelly's shop and Suburban Base label, hardcore and jungle's Essex end.

name: Crazy Beat Records
blurb: Upminster shop at 87 Corbets Tey Road, open almost forty years, with classic house and UK garage among its biggest sellers.

name: Disk Union (Shibuya Club Music Shop)
blurb: The Tokyo chain's club floor in the Antenna 21 building, Udagawacho, with more than 25,000 hip hop, house and techno records.

name: Flashback Records
blurb: Second-hand chain that began on Essex Road, Islington, and added Crouch End in 2006 and Shoreditch in 2014.

name: Hard Wax
blurb: Mark Ernestus's Berlin shop, in Kreuzberg until 2023 and in Mitte since: Basic Channel's counter, the source of Berlin's techno and dub taste, still open.

name: Juno Records
blurb: The online shop that replaced the counter for most of the world, with the distributor-sized catalogue of the 2000s.

name: Lucky Spin
blurb: Jungle shop and label: King's Road, then Holloway Road from 1994; DJ Trace and Harmony worked its counter.

name: Phonica
blurb: Poland Street, Soho: the dance shop of the 2000s and 2010s, still open where Black Market and the rest closed.

name: Record Time
blurb: Roseville, Michigan: the back room where Detroit's second wave bought their imports; Plus 8 and Transmat in the racks.

name: Rounder Records
blurb: Brighton Square shop and ticket outlet where Norman Cook and Skint's Damian Harris both worked; it closed on 29 July 2012.

name: Selectadisc
blurb: Brian Selby's Nottingham shop, where Graeme Park bought the singles; it began on Mansfield market and closed on Market Street.

name: Swag Records
blurb: Croydon shop run by Liz Edwards, with Terry Francis behind the counter, credited by him with the name tech-house.

name: Vinyl Dreams (593 Haight Street)
blurb: Mike Battaglia's dance shop at 593 Haight Street, the below-ground space that was Tweekin Records in the 1990s and 2000s.

name: PK Sound
blurb: Loudspeaker maker founded by Jeremy Bridge and Eroca Colins, directors of Shambhala's Village stage, whose rigs ran all but one of its main stages, by EDM Maniac's account.

name: Black Moon Sound System
blurb: Derbyshire free-party system whose rig was seized near Corby in July 1995 and forfeited in 1996, the first under the 1994 Act by SQUALL's account.

name: Court Acoustics
blurb: Stephen Court's loudspeaker firm of 1973: studio monitors, rock PAs and the Black Box rig that ran Glastonbury's NME Stage in 1994.

name: Sir Coxsone's Downbeat
blurb: Clement Dodd's Kingston sound, stocked with American rhythm and blues from 1953, the root of Studio One.

name: Jah Shaka Sound System
blurb: Neville Powell's south-east London roots reggae sound, 1970–2023: home-made sirens, dubplates and sub-bass that jungle and dubstep DJs later cited.

name: The Levan horn
blurb: Richard Long's sub-bass horn for the Paradise Garage: two 500-watt 18-inch drivers, a 28-square-foot mouth, rated to 30 Hz.

name: Phazon
blurb: New York design and installation company of which Steve Dash was a principal, maker of the PDS subs; systems for Twilo, Vinyl, Cream, Home and crobar.

name: Skan PA
blurb: Hire company that has run Glastonbury's second stage since 1991, with a Court Black Box rig in 1994 and Turbosound Floodlight stock by 1995.

name: Tom the Great Sebastian
blurb: Tom Wong's Kingston sound, from 1950, with Count Machuki on the microphone and Duke Vin selecting.

name: Centreforce 88.3
blurb: East London's seven-day rave station of 1989, by its own claim the first; raided and back on air through the year.

name: Dream FM (Leeds)
blurb: Leeds pirate station where Rachel Fox presented as Daisy & Havoc and a good share of the DJs were women.

name: Kool FM
blurb: The jungle station; Hype, Brockie, Eastman.

name: The Breezeblock
blurb: Mary Anne Hobbs's BBC Radio 1 programme of experimental electronic music, begun on 17 February 1997 and renamed in 2006.

name: YFM
blurb: Johannesburg youth radio station, on air from 1997 with a less-talk, more-tunes format, that rode the wave of kwaito and house.
